CHICAGO, February 11.-Three bot
ties of cheap booze brought three men
face to face with manslaughter charges
today.


Herbert Giers and Anthony Kilberg
were slain early Sunday. following a
traffic quarrel with a colored party.
Parents of the boys. as well as three
youths who were companions of GierS
and Kilberg when the shooting took
place, told the coroner's jury yesterday
that liquor was responsible for the quar-
rel and the shooting.


The youths named Frank Savorski,
John Barry and Joseph pennehy as
men from whom they had purchased
gin and moonshine shortly before the
shooting. The three were to be ar
raigned today before Municipal Judge
William Holmes, who signed the man
slaughter warrants after hearing the
boys stories.


Slayers of Giers and Kilberg have
not been arrested.

BY the Associated Press.


PARIS, June 23.-The first case Of
serious Illness among American Gold
Star Mothers visiting France was re-
vealed yesterday when Mrs. Edwin
Lange Of Oshkosh, Wis, arrived here
suffering from q severe hemorrhage.
She was taken to the American Hos
pital. Physicians said she was in a
very serious condition"


Mrs. Lange suffered the hemorrhage
during the trip across on the liner
President Harding. She was landed on
stretcher at Cherbourg. She was
very weak when she reached Paris, and
physicians indicated she must remain
in the hospital considerable time.


Mrs. Sarah Ann Loomis of Grand
Rapids, Mich, another patient at the
American Hospital, was reported much
better yesterday.

TOXIC, Japan, September 1.-THE
Privy Council Investigation Committee
which has been holding sessions for the
last two months, at today's ANAL meet
ing decided in favor Of recommending
the ratification of the London naval
treaty The approval was accompanied
by warning regarding the supreme
command issue and supplementary naval
defense program.


Count Miyoji Ito, chairman of the
Investigation Committee, will draft the
warning and the report on the discus
sions for submission at a full Privy
Council meeting to be held shortly. The
findings undoubtedly will be concur
red in.


Virtually Ends Conflict.


This virtually terminates the long
draWn-out fight between the govern
ment and the Privy Council and is .
decided victory for the government.
Even up until today the vernacular
press has been predicting dire conse-
quences for the government, with three
possibilities: An indefinite delay due to
lack of adequate information; ratifica-
ton with censure; complete rejection.


The warning regarding the National
defense is merely face-saving for the
privy council and is not of Importance
internationally. The privy council re-
allied that the government had resolved
to ignore any censure, as leading states
men such as Prince Saionji, last sur
viving. "elder" statesman, and Count
Maxine. lord keeper of the privy seal
and public opinion would support the
government, with the result that the
prestige and influence of the privy
council would have been impaired.


Assures Final Ratification.


Today's action assures final ratifica-
ton in the near future and confirms
repeated predictions to this effect. The
privy council has made lots of noise
and has kept in the political limelight,
somewhat resembling the clamor made
in the United States and England, but
in the flnal showdown was forced to
yield under the pressure OF virtually
unanimous support OF the press and
public opinion for the treaty.

may sound queer, but three Jacksonville
residents were taking Pasteur treat
ments today because they ate fish that
had been bitten by a mad dog.


1t happened like this: A man and his
wife, who owned the dog, went fishing
AS fast as they pulled in fish the dog
grabbed it, They thought he was just
being playful.


After they had cooked and eaten the
fish they noticed the dog doing strange
things. They came to the conclusion
that he had hydrophobia.


Then they remembered the fish. The
dog was observed, later killed and found
to be afflicted with rabies.


The man and woman and another
person who had eaten the fish asked the
Health Department what to do. The
Pasteur treatment was prescribed.

anecdote about the shortest part
she ever played. Her appren-
ticeship in the theater was served
with a Washington stock company
and she was once assigned the
role of Polish servant girl whose
only speech was Good morning"
in Polish. Never having studied
that language, Miss Hayes had not
the slightest idea how to pro-
nounce the words. But with the
true artists passion for detail, she
hunted through Washington until
she found a little Polish dress
maker who could give her the cor
rect pronunciation. Miss Hayes
went home and practiced as hard
on her one line of Polish as If it
had been the leading role in the
play.


When she went on the stage at
the opening performance, how
ever, she got stage fright, couldn't
remember the Polish and had to
say Good morning" in plain
English.


This tickled the other actors
immensely since they remembered
how hard she toiled over her tiny
part and it was almost a minute
before they could recover them
selves, choke back their laughter
and go on with the play.

were accepted.

concerned because quantities of arms
were taken from city arsenals during
the fighting Monday night.

VICTORIA, British Columbia.-Can-


ada's west coast is staging a second
sea music festival Wednesday to Sum-
day. So popular were the deep-water
chanteys, the fisher songs and the other
sea music performed at Vancouver just
a year ago that the Canadian Pacific
Railway has sponsored the arrangement
of this second festival here. under the
musical direction of Harold Eustace
Key Randolph Bruce, lieutenant gov
ernor of British Columbia, is keenly
interested in the success of the forth
coming festival. incidentally, British
Columbia has 1000 miles of seacoast.


Important features of last Winters
programs will once again be repeated,
including THE Order of Good Cheer"
a ballad opera Incorporating old French
sea songs of the period of Champlain;
Bound for the Rio Grande," Frederick
William Wallace's sea chantey ballad
opera, and "At a Lewis Fishing" the
fisher folk play written by Ethel Basin
The new attractions will include Hell
bert Heyner, celebrated English bari
tone; John Goss, famous singer of Eng
lish sea chanteys, and UlysSe Paquin,
celebrated French-Canadian basso, who
will sing the sea songs Of Acadia. The
Amphion Choir, pride of Seattle, will
come to Victoria and sing a selection
OF sea music, providing an interesting
comparison with the Arion Choir of
Victoria, the oldest male choir in
Canada.


The old sailor chanteys are supposed
to have died out with the disappear
ance of the sailing ship. but there are
many old-time Canadians who still re-
member those from the days when they
or their parents crossed the Atlantic in
sailing ships and picked them up from
the men who we're working the capstan
or hauling the yards. There are also
old salts still in Canadian ports who
sailed before the mast, to whom these
chanteys are still the greatest Of all
music.

From the time of the building of
the first gasoline engine, the one-cylin-
der effort of Daimler, the chief char
acteristic of the automotive industry
has been vision. Only men of vision
could have chung to the idea of build
ing a perfected gasoline engine when
experts generally were expressing the
opinion that the ultimate vehicle
would be propelled by steam or cleo
tricity. This vision of the perfect gaso-

sively through the one-cylinder, the
two, four and six cylinder cycles, up
to the present, when the improved
eight-cylinder power plant has brought
a new meaning to automobile perform
ance.


Industry Got Start in 1900.


For approximately a decade and a
half after Daimler put his 'one-unger'
into an automobile the single cylinder
motor was the only one known. Ameri-
can inventors took up the idea and cars
were built here. Toward the close of
the one-cylinder cycle the engine was
moved forward under a hood. The
steering wheel and hoat-feed carbure-
tors were installed. The first automo-
bile show was held in 1900 and the in
duStry got its real start there.


Smoother performance has always
been the aim of American manufac-
turers, along with economy of operation
and low cost. While European inventors
have the credit for much Of the early
development, it was in this country that
the idea of individual transportation as
an everyday convenience for every one
grew most rapidly.


1.-The 'one-lunger' gave way to two
cylinders. Somewhat smoother per-
Torrance was the result The next
cycle. a few years later, was inaugu-
rated by the four-cylinder motor and
greatly improved smoothneSs. It was
a sensational advance. All manufac-
turers rushed into four cylinders and
the gasoline automobile became a fix
ture. The experts who had predicted
steam or electricity as the ultimate mo-
tive power were Silenced.


Costs Are Reduced.


"Still seeking a smoother, quieter,
more flexible engine, experimentation
continued, with six and eight cylin-
ders. The six burst almost as suddenly
as the four upon the automobile mar
ket. Its merits were soon demonstrated
Velvet performance became a funda-
mental requirement for good automo-
bile


"Eight-cylinder cars were built, some
abroad. some here, but many engineer
ing difficulties were encountered and
the Fights were expensive. They were
to be found only among the luxury cars.
Constant experimentation, however,
eliminated imperfections and the won
derful development of the last few
years in manufacturing methods has
brought down the cost of production.

text:
Final enactment of the tariff,
passage of prohibition reforms
and disposition. of the Govern
ment's 100000. 900 Muscle Shoals
project were the important legis-
lative problems pending in Con-
gress today as both House and
Senate rested over the weekend.


When these three measures are
added to tax reduction, farm re-
lief and the enlarged Federal
construction program, Congress
will hike home for the approach
ing congressional elections. All
the legislation and politics of the
last year or ever since Herbert
Hoover moved into the White
House, will be fuel and fodder
Tor the individual campaigns.


Plan to Adjourn June


Administration leaders are plan
ming adjournment about June i,
but the estimates ranged all the
way from May IS to July /. The
date actually will depend upon
the time when House and Senate
agree upon their tariff differ
ences, with Congress adjourning
probably within two weeks after
President Hoover signs the tariff
bill.


Before House and Senate can
agree on the tariff, their con-
fereeS must iron out several major
disputes. These involve the flex-
1ble tariff provision, which the
Senate repealed, the debenture
form of farm relief the Senate put
In the bill, and the conflicting
rates on sugar, cement, lumber,
logs. bricks, watches, clocks, hides
leather, shoes, wool, glass, pigiron,
and aluminium. The conferees
alone will consume at least two
weeks compiling a report and it
may require months before House
and Senate agree to it.


Muscle Shoals.


The muscle Shoals bill will start
its long journey through Congress
In the Senate Tuesday. It may
pass during the week, but it will
meet stiff opposition in the House.
There were strong probabilities
the Senate would give the govern
ment some preference in operating
the project for the present, even
though a strong bloc favorS a
straight out lease to private inter
ests. The pending bill would pre-
vide for preferential sale of all sur.
plus power to cities and states.
This provision will meet serious
opposition.


The prohibition reform bills
have been in the House. One,
transferring the prohibition
bureau from the Treasury to the
Department of Justice, has passed
the House and awaits Senate
action. The other bills, amend
ing the Jones Act. reducing minor
penalties and changing court
procedure to relieve congestion,
were still on the House calendar.
The President has asked for their
passage before Congress adjourns.
Senate Dry Probe


All these measures must pass
the Senate, where a demand mas
been made for thorough in
vestigation of prohibition enforce
ment before any legislation is
enacted. The Senate Judiciary
Committee will meet Monday,
probably to hear Attorney Gen
eral William D. Mitchell on the
proposed inquiry. Regardless of
his advice, part Of the committee
will urge a Senate inquiry. If
the inquiry is started, all prohibi-
ton legislation probably will be
Sidetracked until the next session
of Congress.


This would merely hasten the
date OF adjournment. At any
rate, Congress must dispose of
the tariff. the prohibition bills
and Muscle Shoals, one way or
another, before going home.

By the Associated Press.


WOOSTER, Ohio, January 4.-Help-
less victims of speeding train which
cut through the night and a binding
sleet storm to crush their bus while they
laughed and talked Of their basket bal
games, seven youths were dead anc
eight other high school boys and girl.
were in hospitals today.


The dead boys, all of them between
IA and Is years of age, were members
Of the high school basket ball team OF
Burbank, near here. They we're on then
way home, happy over defeating theil
old rivals at Big Prairie, another nearb,
village, when Pennsylvania Railroad
flyer struck their bus at q crossing
near Shreve, 10 miles south Of here, last
night.


The dead are:


Wilbur and Forest Grubb, brothers.


Claude Repp.


Wayne Lehman.


Emil Timic.


Eugene Talley.


Willard Baker.


Most Seriously Hurt.


The most seriously injured were
Edith Repp, who suffered fractures of
both legs and may die, and Lola Talley
sister Of the dead boy, who received a
broken leg.


The others injured, most of whom
suffered nothing more serious than cuts
ana bruises, are Charles Packard, DON
aid Lehman, Alice West, Ellen Cowhick
Grace Flory, Maurice Lenz, coach of
the burbank team. and Joseph Baker,
so, driver Of the bus.


The crumpled bus was carried down
the track 100 feet, and bodies were
strewn four times that distance as the
banter and gayety. of the youngsters
was changed to shrieks and the smash
ing OF steel and splintering of wood.
AmbulanceS were called from Wooster,
and raced perilously over the ice-cov-
cred highway to take the injured to
Woosters two hospitals.


Bus Driver Overcome.


Baker, the bus driver, was overcome
and unable to give any coherent ex-
PLANTATION Of what happened. He could
not remember whether he stopped be-
fore climbing the incline to the cross
ging. The crossing at the hour of the
accident-after 10 o'clock-is protected
only by bell and flash signal. Coach
Lenz and those of the injured who were
able to talk likewise did not know what
occurred before the rushing train was
upon them. Pennsylvania Railroad Of
t1cialS at Shere said apparently Baker
had not seen the train coming through
the storm and started across directly
In front of It,


The tragedy hit hard at Burbank, a
town Of only 500 people Every one
knew the boys and girls on the basket
bal teams and many had journeyed to
root for them at Big Prairie. The
rooters started home ahead of the
players, who had to have time to
change clothese, eager to tell how the
boys team had defeated their old
enemies, although the girls lost.


Word Of the accident Travelled rapidly,
however, and soon the hospitals and
undertaking establishments here were
filled with the better part of Burbank'S
residents, mothers and fathers rushing
anxiously from place to place to find
their sons and daughters. The rooters,
who had turned back, were joined by
many others who hastily started for
Wooster when, instead of accounts of
the games, they received the messages
OF death.

CHICAGO, February 12.-Another
terrific explosion shook the North Side
last night, Two people were injured
the rear of the building housing the
Northwestern Laundry Co. was wrecked
and the damage was estimated at more
than $4,000.


At first attributed to bursting boiler,
Fire Department officials later found
the boilers intact and said the explosion
was caused by bomb.


Several hours later, far across the city
on the South Side, second bomb was
exploded beneath the bed room window
OF William Roberts, a trucking con-
tractor. The house was damaged and
nearby windows shattered.


The North Side explosion rocked the
business district at the intersection of
Lincoln avenue and Diversey Parkway.
Hundreds of windows were broken and
automobiles were covered with glass and
debris.


The explosion, occurring at 1920
pm, attracted several thousand people
One woman walking on a street to the
rear Of the laundry was struck by flying
glass and her head badly cut. A man
driving a truck past the alley entrance
was hurled to the ground when the
windshield of his truck was blown in.


The owners of the laundry were I'M
able to account for the explosion. Their
truck drivers were all union men and
they had no trouble, they said.


With all windows blown out of their
homes, many families in the neighbor-
hood were forced to seek other shelter
for the night.


Roberts also said he had had no labor
trouble and could not account for the
bombing of his home. He and his wife
were thrown from bed, but were not
injured.

BEACON, N. Y, December 4.-Three
men, armed with guns, invaded Matte
wan State Hospital for the Criminal
Insane early today, overpowered four
employees and liberated six inmates.


The leader Of the gang was recog-
nized as a former inmate by hospital
attendants, who said he was william
Nelson Of New York.


The six who were liberated were:
Harry Gordon, SO, Rochester; Frank
Danberkeylen, 81, New York; Joseph
Kaylor, IS, the Bronx; John 8. Bangill,
az, New York; John higgins, 30, Brook
Ign; Anthony A. Elloy, A, Brooklyn.


DR.. Raymond F. c. Kieb, superin-
tendent, said the three men entered the
hospital grounds through the rear yard,
where they encountered Patrick Nc
Grath, the night Waterman, and COM
PEELED him to accompany them.


Cook Forced to Join Gang.


In the kitchen they came upon Cliff
ford Cooper, night cook, forcing him to
Join them. They continued through the
building toward the front, where they
picked up Joseph Brown, the rounds
man. Then they herded their prison.
ers into the front ONCE, where Samuel
Kane, the night ofice man, was on duty.


While one Of them guarded their
prisoners the other two went to the
front dormitory where the six men were
In bed. The six apparently were watch
ing for them, DR.. Kieb said, for as soon
as the intruders appeared they sprang
UP from their cots and ran out, two Of
them clad only in night attire. They
drove away in two automobiles.


Knew Hospital Routine.


DR.. Kieb said the escape would not
have been possible had It not been for
Nelson's knowledge of the hospital
routine. He knew where to find the
various employees and how to surprise
them one at time.


The superintendent said those who
escaped were not known as dangerous,
but were suffering from mental diseases
which manifest themselves in extreme
cunning.

BOISE, Idaho, August l9.-Investi-

ago near King Hill, Idaho, has resulted
in the arrest of her foster father, H. B.
Miesenzal1l, and his wife.

Penitentiary here for safekeeping. Both
Miesenzahl and his wife deny any con-
nection with the death of the child,
whom they adopted two years ago.


The girl was seized along railroad
track, a mile from home, dragged into
A patch of willows near the brink OF
the Snake River and assaulted. Her
throat was cut, and the body was
thrown into the river, weighted down
by stone.

The foster father was circumstantial,
but he asserted that Mrs. Miesenzahl
was aware her husband had been mis-
treating the child before the day Of the
murder.

Good mashed potatoes may be made
by this method:


Select potatoes of about the same

potatoes are almost done. Then pour
off all but cupful of the water, cover
the pan securely, and place it over a
low flame to steam. When the potatoes
are perfectly tender, take of the cover
and let the water evaporate.


Have ready a cupful of top milk or
thin cream, heated in a double boiler.
Mash the potatoes, adding the hot, rich
milk. Add plenty of butter and just
enough salt and pepper. When the
potatoes are well mashed, beat with a
big egg beater until they are creamy,

ned at the sudden turn of foot ball

BY the Associated Press.


TOXIC, September 23.-Rengo dis
patches from Peiping today said the
ancient Chinese capital was in full
possession of Manchurian troops.


Trainload after trainload of Mukden-
tie units were brought within the walls
of the old capital It was learned q
portion of these forces will be dis
patched northwestward along the Piep-
ing-Suiyuan Railway as far as Kalgan
and others down the Peiping- Hankow
Railway as far as Paotingfu.


Suspicion was strong that Chang
Hsueh-Liang. 80 years old, dictator of
Manchuria, would attempt to set up his
own government in Peiping. as his
father. Chang Tso-Lin, often did in
descents from his capital at Mukden.


Strikes at Crucial Time.


Chang struck when northern rebel
and Nationalist government troops were
exhausted by six months of internecine
warfare and unable to make marked
gains. Although claimed by the Ma
tionalists as their ally since May, he had
remained aloof until the time came to
become the deciding factor.


For the present the civil war appears
ended Gems. Yen Hsi-Shan and Feng
Yu-Hsiang, leaders of the NorthernerS,
are heading their armies from Pieping
toward Taiyuan, the Shansi province
capital of Gov. Yen.


Many students of China affairs pre-
dicted Yen and Feng would encamp in
Shansi Mountains, gathering strength
for another onslaught upon the govern
ment. If they did this they would be
repeating their action of last December,
when they withdrew their armies from
Honan after exacting heavy tribute from
the Marking government.


Rewards Are Hinted.


Reports were current Chang Hsueh-
LANG had received Chill Province, In
Guiding Peiping and Tientsin, and
100000 from the Nationalist as
reward for his intervention.


Other reports were Chang would act
independently and attempt to extend
his rule from Manchuria south to the
Yellow River Although believed to
entertain this belief, Nationalist oficials
acclaimed Changes occupation of Peip-
ing as a triumph for the Central gov
eminent.


One concrete fact stood out: One
trainload of the 5000 Manchurian SOL
oilers had entered Peiping, while other
trains were nearing the old capital,
having passed Langfang and were less
than so miles from their goal


Peiping civilians, accustomed to
change of war lords, hastened to declare
loyalty to the new ruler and conditions
were peaceful. Even the Northern rebel
leaders, Fastening to safety, stated their
intention Of maintaining friendly rela-
tons with the Manchurian, but, they
said, they were steadfast in their inten-
ton to overthrow the Nationalist
regime.

NEW ORLEANS, February 15.-Few
people realize it. but New Orleans still
has street car strike dating back from
July 2. The only reminders are an
occasional popping of of homemade
bombs on street car rails. These ex-
plosions are passed off with a shrug.


Cars are operating on schedule with
heavy patronage. Most of the regular
motormen and conductors have gone
back to work. At first New Orleans
was enthusiastically behind the strikers.
Mobs of hundreds of men and women
stormed the Offices. barns and cars of
the New Orleans Public Service, Inc.
They bore down with stones, sticks and
guns and it was worth ones life to
ride street car six months ago. Two
men were dragged out of mob fights
dying and hundreds were bruised and
manned. Canal street became q bat
tle-ground for pillagers and rioters,
strike-breakers and police. Property
damage ran into the thousands and
business was demoralized.


Then came the Federal Injunction
prohibiting interference with car oper-
alton and damage to company prop
erty. Special deputies and SQUADS of
police were sent out to enforce it with
Shotguns.


Meantime, officials of the Garments
Union were negotiating for settlement
and definite terms were reached at a
conference in New York between Pub
lie Service oficialS and William D.
Mahon, international president of the
Street Garments Union, and William
Green, president Of the American Fed
Grafton of Labor. But the men voted
down the agreement unless the Public
Service would agree to take back all of
the strikers at once. Public Service re-
fused to amend the terms and issued
an ultimatum to the strikers. The
union ignored the warning and Mr..
Mahon and Mr.. Green stepped aside
Weeks later the men voted to accept
the New York terms, but Public Serv-
ice refused to deal further with the
union Large numbers Of strikers ap-
piled for their old jobs.

The fastest idea in industrial rail-
ways is the plant which has been de-
signed for the Trinity Portland Cement
Co. Railway cars without passengers
and apparently running without human
energy will transfer cement rock from
the excavating pit to the crusher on a
railway haulage system. Two operators,
located where they can view the load
ing and unloading of the cars and their
movements, govern practically all the
operations of the cars. The track on
which the cars will run will be divided
into number of sections. Four motor
driven cars will ride over the track,
each propelled by two 50-horsepoWer
motors. Energy for driving the motors
will be supplied from the track and
third-rail system Thus by energizing
all the sections of the track the cars
will run from one end to the other,
The cars will be stopped by interrupt
ing the electric current to the section
on which the cars are travelling. Elec-
trio brakes, operating automatically
will stop the car when the energy sup
ply is interrupted. An interesting char
acteristic of the motors operating the
cars is that they will tend to main
tain constant speed under all circum-
stances. On down grades the motors
will act as generator and the electricity
thus generated will be fed back into the
power system, helping to operate other
cars on other sections Of the track.

Cheated of all but two victims among
the 80 men trapped in the smoke-fllled
tunnels, flames Tapped stubbornly away
today in the depths Of the Wolf Run
mine of the Warner collieries near
Amsterdam, rs miles from here.


Sparks from the electric trolley pole
of train started confiagration which
for hours threatened major mine
disaster, but heroic rescue squads, pick
ing their way through tongues Of flames
springing from timbers and coal,
brought every man but two safely to
the surface.


Paul Borkowski, IS, died soon after
he was brought OUT He suffered from
asthma and could not survive the chok-
ing coal fumes he had breathed. The
body of Jack PewoSki, 81, was found


Two Rescuers Collapse.


Another miner, George Altman, was
severely burned on the; feet, legs and
hips while daShing across a barrier OF
fire. Two rescuers, Sidney Wales and
Arnold Horton, inspectors of the mine,
collapsed from exhaustion after tramp
ing for miles to search for workmen.


The 81 others cut of by the blaze
were brought out unframed, although
20 of them owed their lives to the des-
perste work of the Steubenville Fire De-
partment and mine rescue squads.
About q dozen of them were uncon-
SctouS from the intense heat and smoke
when carried to the surface, but most
of them were able to walk to their
nearby homes after they had been re-
vived. Company officials announced at
midnight that every man had been &C
counted for.


The fire broke out about 1000 feet
back from the main entrance shaft yes
terday afternoon, and telephone COM
munication to the mines was destroyed.


Prevented Blockade.


The Steubenville Fire Department
made 25-mile run and began pumping
water just in time to save the weak
ened timberS from allowing dirt and
shale to slide in and block the trapped
men. About 70 men were threatened,
the rest having been able to escape or
were brought out before the flames
could cut them OF.


For a time it seemed that the FIRE
would be the victor, but five hours later
it was checked sufficiently that res
cuers, wearing gas masks, crept through
and brought out 10 men, exhausted and
gasping for air. 1t was believed the
trapped men lived because fresh air had
constantly been pumped through an
overcast chute.


The rescue was made barely in time,
for less than three hours later the flames
again gained Roadway and, Fire Chief
Edward Green of Steubenville said he
feared it would be impossible TO save
the mine from destruction. Shifts of
firemen were kept at their posts all
night.

The sad thing about his life WA that not even
all his holidays were passed at this beloved
home.


THE first Christmas spent at Mount Vernon


by its future owner was in the year I747,
with his elder half-brother, Lawrence WASH
ington. Here the young lad was initiated into
the English manner of living, his brother hav-
ing married Anne Fairfax, whose family at
Greenway Court nearby, remained English to
the core, and drank to the kings health long
after the Revolution.


After the early death of this beloved brother
and his only child, George Washington con-
tmued to spend the greater part of his HOLIDAYS
with the family at Greenway Court, but only
few years elapsed after his establishment as
the owner of Mount Vernon before he accepted
the call to defend his country under Gen Brad
dock. When he came home for good as he
thought, from this service he brought with
him legacy from Gen. Braddock-the good
Servitor Thomas Bishop. who waited on George
Washington with rare devotion as long as life
permitted. 1t was Bishop who held the horses
and who arrayed George Washington in all his
wedding bravery.


Not perhaps the most splendid and notable
ChristmasSeS at Mount Vernon-those came
after the Revolution and when he had returned
later still from the Presidency, secure forever
as the deliver Of their country and the FIRST
in their hearts-but the most peaceful happy
Christmases, untouched by sorrow and young
and carefree at Mount Vernon were those fol-
lowing his marriage to the eminently attractive
and worthy Martha Gusts, when he had the
two little children to make Christmas for him
and he for them. There was no halfway
business about this man. When he married
the mother, the children became his to love
and cherish This renowned man found his
greatest happiness in his home and family
Had the lines Stay, stay at home my heart,
and rest: Housekeeping hearts are happiest"
been written in his time Washington would
have loved them. He never left his home
without great regret and never returned without
the greatest delight.


Mount Vernon began to grow, the acreage in
creased, farm after farm was laid OF, and the
house became a mansion, filed with beautiful
things, the intelligent owner realizing that
the purchase Of the best only is true economy.
It was not, however, until after the Revolution
that Mount Vernon attained its full glory.
These were busy years, requiring unerring judg-
ment and the great industry Of the master
to make the land support the three hundred
and odd slaves and the numerous bonded and
free white employees necessary. The tobacco
crop, the crop that made America dear to
England was depended on to bring the choicest
Of English supplies, necessities and luxuries,
clothing, food, books, toys, furniture as its ex-
change value.


Historians consider that Martha Washington
was perhaps too dotingly fond and indulgent,
their turn came, and instance her husband 40
the perfect parent wise loving, lenient If pos
sible, and always with an understanding heart.

The welfare and happiness of these two little
children was most dear to him. and their needs
and desires always received the most active
consideration sweet, happy home, peace,
plenty children and friends.


Certain it is that, though sometimes found
awe-inspiring and unapproachable by those not
intimately connected with him, Washington
VNs most considerate Of the rights Of others
and recognized by children their friend. Afar
of little ones were taught to say his name in
reverence, but those within his circle sat on
his knee and were told Aesop:S Fables and

trucks in New York, while three-fifths
of those along pavements operate them.

ments drove their trucks an average Of
725 miles more year than the farmers
served by dirt roads.


This indicates that the rural districts
served by pavements have been able to
market their produce farther away

prices. The Cornell survey points out
that the farmer living along the dirt road

local market. Farmers on paved roads,
however, have their choice of three
markets; city markets, local markets or
shipping points, or buyers who come to
the farm.

rectifying plant and conf1scated 1000
gallons of whisky and champaign,

~ OSTON, August 2.-Young Bill

mo one in Dutch Guiana seems hur-.

sturdy Guiana Indians, Chinese in

Special Dispatch to The Star.


ALEXANDRIA, Va, March 29.--Two
white men about rs years Of age,
strolled into the Sanitary Grocery store
at Braddock Station near here tonight,
pulled a gun on three clerks and two
customers and robbed the cash drawer
Of $50.


The clerks were herded into the back
of the store by one OF the stick-up men,
while the other took the cash from
the drawer. Then the clerks were
forced to turn their pockets inside out,
but no money was found.


George Henderson of Rosemont,
manager of the store, outwitted the
thieves when asked to disclose the con-
tents of his pockets. He turned out
all but one pocket and that contained
more than 500 in bills which was
saved. Shortly before the robbers en-
tered, the manager had placed large
amount of money in the safe.


The two customers were ignored by
the robbers, after being told to stand
aside and keep out Of the way. Mar
shall Evans, one of the clerks, was
waiting on these two customers when
the robbers entered, and was directed to
finish with them before he joined the
others in the back Of the store. VIII
liam Burroughs was the other clerk


The robbery completed, the two men
hurriedly left the store and were last
seen headed toward Glendale. Police.
led by Detective Sergt Edgar Sims and
Sergts. Thompson and Padgett investi-
gated the affair. This is the second
robbery at this store recently.

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, August 19.-Just like
molasses will invariably attract flies, so
falling security markets attract swim
dlers. The writer. within two weeks
after the Autumn crash, had pointed
out to him some of the most notorious
bucketeers that ever set foot on Wall
Street. They rested while the stock
market scared dizzily, for a bucket
shop never makes money in a rising
market, but these vultureS returned here
from their European. South American
and Canadian haunts rs soon as shares
crashed.


Customers OF fraudulent security con-
Germs have lost about $37,010,000 in the
last seven months, of which nearly
100000 was lost in July. Unlike
other bear" markets, however, fraud
ulent security sellers have met increas-
ing sales resistance and persistent
persecution from both Federal and State
authorities.


One of the most cheerful items in
the monthly report of the New York
State Bureau of Securities today is the
increasing number of prosecutions. The
bureau obtained 90 show cause orders
against So individuals, firms and cor
porations during July, compared with 8
such actions against 36 individuals and
firms in July, 1929.


The outstanding achievement of the
Stock Exchange since the turn of the
century has been its successful war
against security Swindlers. Realizing
that bucketShop patrons had no effect
marketWise, since neither their sales
nor purchases ever were executed.
the exchange deliberately fought the
vultures that prey on the gullible per-
sons that visit the financial district.
Purely aside from stimulating trading
the volume OF exchange dealings rose
about rs per cent with the wiping out
of bucketshops as the hinterland found
Wall Street to be predominantly
honest-the New York Stock Exchange
has saved millions for the average in
vestor through It's constant war on
security crooks.

ing for several moments, and in the

ing the occupant against the window

ing the stool firmly with nonskid ma
terial under it. They learned that at
the lecture.

No emigrant ever adapted himself so
quickly to American standards of living
as the tiny alien who recently arrived
in the Burleith residential section,
causing much hilarity among the chill
dren Of the neighborhood by his strange
chatter and queer little face, but quick
ly winning their hearts by his playful
ness and friendly manners.


A little more than a year ago Coco"
was climbing trees and eating bananas
in the Jungles of Nicaragua. His ST.
milan mother must have been careless,
for Coco was but baby and should
have been watched to see that he did
not wander too far from the family tree.
This is what happened, however, as one
fine day Coco lost his way in the jungle
and he was found by a Marine, who
carried him to the quarters of Capt.
william Carvel Hall at Puerto Cabezas,
where the captain recently had been
joined by Mrs. Hall and his two little
daughters Petsy and Mimi Perhaps,
thought the Marine, the captains little
girls would like Coco as a pet.


When Capt Hall received orders re-
lieving him from duty in Nicaragua to
report for duty in Washington, Patsy
and Mimi we're obliged to leave beau
tiful macaw and a cage full of para
keets behind, but nothing could have
parted FaJSy lIOIn OOCO. All IaCbs hOtIl-
ing could have parted Coco from any
of the Hall family. Placed in
a large parrot cage, the little fellow
was taken aboard the steamer which
carried him and his family to New
Orleans.


Since his arrival in the United States,
Coco has developed strong liking for
American foods, his real weakness being
cereals and milk with plenty Of sugar
Yes, Coco certainly was born with q
sweet tooth. When his little mistress
prepares his cereal, should she neglect to
sweeten it with sufficient sugar, no one
can look more unhappy than Coco, who
grumbles and chatters until they pass
him the sugar bowl.


. Grapes and apples, and all the fruits
which could never grow in tropical
jungle, are the foods Coco likes best.
He hates bananas, which goes to prove
they must have been the principal form
Of diet in the jungle.


Coco, who was named for the Coco
river, where Capt. Hall was stationed
for some time, now lives in his own
little house in the back yard of the
Halls home, 1925 T street.

Furious gales accompanied by tor
rental transforms dashed the European
continent today, taking at least nine
lives, inflicting serious injury upon
hundreds, and wreaking havoc in
France, Belgium, Germany and Austria.


Belgium appeared to be the heaviest
sufferer, Tor her low countryside was
inundated when swollen rivers topped
the dikes and oyerran the fields.
- A wind of hurricane force swept
Vienna, where three persons were killed,
q seriously injured and many others
slightly hurt.


French rivers overlooked their banks
and France was under water from
Havfe to Paris. Navigation of the
Seine was impossible and such vessels
as could not md shelter were damaged
or sunk. sOne girl was reported
drowned. o., .-..


Thousands Routed in Germany.


Germany was hard hit. In the south
the Rhine and MoSelle overran4 their
banks, driving thousands from their
homes to higher land. At Friedrich
shafen, home Of the Graf Zeppelin, and
throughout the Lake Constance region,
hurricanes did tremendous damage.


The storm extended even to Spain,
and at Corunna the German seaplane
Do-X was unable to continue a flight
to Lisbon.


The English Channel and waters
along the coast of Europe were q con-
slant menace to shipping.


TWO steamships caught in the gale
which swept the English Channel were
almost driven on the rocky coast, but
escaped disaster under their own power
after several rescue vessels, including a
navy cruiser, had gone to their aid.
: The Greek steamers Triton and
Taxiarchis got into trouble of Port
land, but ran clear Of danger as the
wind abated.


Property Damage Enormous.


Thousands were made homeless in
France, Belgium and Germany, prop
erty damage was enormous. Emergency
flood measures appeared to be useless
and the rains continued pouring down
today.


Paris was worried. High walls run
the length of the city as a protection
against floods, but the water was rising
steadily toward the top of these en-
bankments. The Marine Canal was a
tangled mass of barges from which
produce, could not be unloaded.


In the Seine dozens of tug boats were
caught between bridges because they
could not pass under with the water at
its present level.


Like all i'll winds, however, this one
blew some good to the unemployed, who
were impressed into service for the
emergency as builders of temporary
bridges and reScuers of the homeless.


A terrific gale swept the Loire Valley
today, leveling trees and unroofing
houses Many persons were reported
injured.

RIGA, September 19.-Latvian observ-
ers on the Russian border report that
conditions at present are similar to those
earlier in the year when the Russian
peasantry began great exodus in pro-
test against the forcible collectivization
of their lands-a measure which was
later suspended.


The harvest and the program for new
sowings have been so unsuccessful in
Russia that the Moscow government hes
modified 5000 students for work on
the collective farms. The collectors are
communicating grain from both the
peasants and the collective farms along
the border, where observers have heard
the sound of rifle shots and received re-
ports that peasants were being killed
and their houses burned.


Frontier guards are making renewed
preparations for a mass fight of the
peaSantry over the Latvian border.

A most unusual art exhibition re-
Gently was opened at Oslo, Norway. with
the late Prof. Fridtjof Nansen as sole
exhibitor. He was an ardent lover of
art and during his lifetime made nu-
merous drawings, water colors and pas
tells. His intimate friend, the famous
Norwegian painter, Erik Werenskiold,
and his Son-in-law, and the reputed
painter, Prof. Revold after Nansen's
death, selected about 100 of the most
representative examples of his art and
now the public for the first time has
an opportunity to learn still q new side
of this richly gifted personality.


Most of the pictures are astonishingly
small in size. II often told Mr.. Nam
sen to make his cartoons larger" says
Prof. Werenskiold. but he has always
refused, fearing one might think him
pretentious."


The exhibition shows that this fear
was unfounded. The pictures are con-
sidered masterpieces and one of them
portrays Prof. Nansen sitting on his
knees playing with his 4-year-old
grandchild. The earliest picture of the
exhibition dates back to the savant's
early youth, Many were made during
his polar expeditions. The latest pic
ture was finished only q few days be-
fore his death.

August 9, I861.-The United States
steamer Freeborn, commanded by Lieut..
Hurld. arrived at the Washington Navy
Yard from the lower Potomac River
this morning, for coal and other sup
plies, and left this afternoon.
The Freeborn is now engaged in
cruising between Fort Washington and
Auuia Greek. on the Potomac River,
and running into the little inlets and
creeks, overhauling and destroying
boats. All boats of which satisfac-
tory account is not given are summary
DESTROYED. thereby very much impairing
the facilities for communication be-
tween the Maryland and Virginia
shores.


Occasionally a shot or shell is
tossed over onto Matthias Point. Va,
and other places where the Confed-
crates are supposed to be, but there
has been no reply.


Night before last the George Page,
Confederate vessel, attempted to run
out of Aqua Greek, but the Ice Boat
engaged her and, after a brief period
of firing, during which only a few
shots were exchanged, the Confederate
vessel returned up the creek out of
range of the Union guns.


The Ice Boat was not struck and it
is not certain whether the Page was hit.
Inc rage carries SIX guns and Is
said to have been painted black. She
frequently shows her daring by coming
down to the mouth of Aqua Creek, and
usually goes back to her den" after a
brief look around.


The Ice Boat and the Pocaho
now guard that point for the Federal
Navy. They occasionally drop a shell
into the woods, in order to test the
range.


The Pawnee and the brig Perry
Union vessels-lie in the Potomac River
off Alexandria. Several vessels, taken
by the Union vessels as pri3rs from the
Confederates, lie off the wharf at Fort
Washington, Md.

To the Editor of The Star:


Washington school children are Diff
fering about what constitutes i'm
morality!


Is it any wonder that there are these
individual differences, since their ideas
and impressions of the world are the
sum total of their education and train
ing, their experience and local environ
ment? Graded and high school pupils
represent different rates and degrees Of
mental achievement. Therefore, they
must decide their moral and ethical
problems differently. Even in the same
families, no two children have the same
degree of education and training, or ex-
perience with life, and so no two can
be expected to hold the same views and
opinions about social matters. nor can
the same way. Then, too when parents,
relatives, friends are governed by ex-
actly the same social factors, and rep
resent practically the same differences
of opinion, how can children help hav-
ing such marked intellectual differences?


There never has been any marked
general agreement about social affairs
and problems among boys and girls Of
school age and, doubtless. there never
will be. How can we expect mere chill
dren and adolescents to have the same
ideas about such questions as planting
trees along United States highways,
identifying the city of Washington,
educating school children of Washing
ton, working out new system of traf-
fic control, or about many other local
and national problems? Clearly, we
cannot when their "grown-ups," for the
very same social reasons, differ about
the tariff, the next United States Sen
ator or governor, or perhaps about the
moon. WERNER M. HOLSTON.

that took her too often from her friends

self, strangely, though, even in the tale,

lay down quietly to await the final

Story Of Thirteen Cigarettes.

the Thirteen Cigarettes" tells Of the
death of all that was mortal Of Draper
Gill. 1t follows:


October 81, 1880

1.-THE bare attic room bore signs OF

sufficiently interesting to fire any ones
imagination. Discolored, once-white
walls, the plaster Clipped and cracked,
and a few nail holes were about all.
Situated on the fourth and top floor
and partitioned OF from the unfinished
attic proper, the room had probably
been occupied by careless servants.


carol lay prone on a cot in this
same room, ostensibly reading but stop
ping at intervals to rehearse what had
become very futile philosophy Of life
her life.


Termed CONN Nails.


"Just the other day she had read q

pen,' but nothing had In the story.
Carol had been more fortunate in the
past, and the evil spells of desirable
circumstances have always been broken
sooner or later. Now it was different.
She was 26 and voluntarily or involun-

Reviewing events, recent and long

childish spontaneity had been half
smothered during adolescence and
thoughtless selfishness coupled with an
indefinable weakness Of purpose were

tesuuely Little spurts of dust rose from the
dry earth before him and behind; Gathering
of fiat reports came from the hillside. Once he
seemed to falter; he swerved like drunken
man; then he ran on. He gained the pony's
side; they saw him swing into the saddle and
ride away.


Lee slammed the door and dropped the bar
into its place. moment later the Apaches
came again.


How long that rush lasted the three within
the building never knew. 1t seemed like hours
before the uncanny silence had settled down
once more. The two men took stock of their
cartridges. Twelve rounds remained. Ed Samp-
son was ransacking his vocabulary for some
epithet sufficiently vile to convey his opinion Of
Kettle. Now and again, discovering one that
promised we'll he whispered it to himself He
might have spoken aloud without danger of
Eileen overhearing.


She was standing beside Lee; her head was
on his breast, his arms were holding her close
She had come to him without word. There
was no word spoken between them now. So
they stood until the ugly fiat voices of the rifles
called him back to his window.


An hour later Lee was kneeling by the win
dow; his empty rifle lay on the floor, his re-
volver was in his hand. Two cartridges were
left In the cylinder. He had been waiting for
dreary time in expectation of the next rush.
It would be the final closing in; there was no
doubt Of that. But for some reason of their
own, the Apaches were still holding back His
eyes went to Eileen; she was standing in the
corner whittier he had sent her at the begin
ning-ages ago it seemed to him now-and her
eyes were on him. That look of theirs was as a
last embrace.


One cartridge for her, one for himself. when


Suddenly the venomous chorus of the rifles
began. leaden slug ricocheted from the wall
beside the window, showering his face with
fragments Of rock and hot metal, leaving him

across his eyes. They were at the front of the
building now; he could hear their yells through
the firing as they swept upon the place to
overwhelm them. His vision cleared; there
came rush of footsteps and the open space

that down-river rum-runners have turn
ed to kidnapping because of unfavorable
conditions in the importing" business
Is being investigated today by detectives
Of the Detroit police Blackhand squad
In their search for Charles Kaier, re-

held since last Thursday night by kid
napers.


Inspector John Hoffman, head Of the

passage of the Canadian law forbid

States rum-runners have turned to
shaking down" wealthy persons who,
FOR various reasons, would not appeal

found this less hazardous than run
ming liquor across the river, up to the
last few days. However, threats rather
than acts have been used to obtain

Kaier was taken from his home

district attorneys Office. Shortly after
her husband left with the men Mrs.

for $4,000 ransom. She did not COM
municate with police, but managed to

Detectives learned of the kidnapping

trailed Mrs. Kaier to hotel, where she
went to deliver $4,000 of the ransom
money. She waited several hours Sat-
Irday afternoon and night, but the kid
napers agent failed to appear. Two
detectives sat in the lobby near the
womal and others were waiting in the
street Mrs. Kaier went home in an
historical condition, and neighbors
called police.


Inspector Hoffman said that Joseph
(Peajacket) Wozniak, alleged rum-run
ner, indicted two years ago in connec-
ton with the bribing of two-score Dor
der customs patrolmen, called at the
Kaier home several times and finally
was taken into custody for questioning
Entrance of Wozniak into the case led
Hoffman to believe that Kaier was &C
quainted with rum-runners and Is held

THE traveller must mingle with the
natives on the streets of villages and
towns that dot the island and bounce
with them over gracefully winding roads
In springlesS oxcarts to get the genuine
atmosphere Of Terceira.


"Angra, the capital Of Terceira, and
largest city on the island, was the capt.
tai OF the Azores until the early part of
the last century. Since then it has
seen few changes. From Angra Bay,
Angra presents splash of color-clus-

Vermillion and blue tile roofs, nesting
Snugly at the base of massive gray
fortress walls that, in the heyday of the
cltys political power, made the capital
safe from attack.

Even the scows and rowboats dot
ting the Angra anchorage are graceful

hoist and parked autos lend q modern

nance. The peddler leads q drowsy DON
key, whose slow movements seem to
protest against q burden Of baskets of
oranges, lemons, pomegranates and -ba-
nanaS.


Goat carts and sheep carts that any
american boy would like to own weave
IN ana out OF Angra traflc The little
fellows draw riders several times their
size and weight and loads of grain and
other produce tax the strength of their
frail legs.


."One would gather from the number
OF oxcarts seen on Terceira that this is
the national vehicle of the island
With bodies like huge woven-reed wash
baskets set between two thick crude
wheels, they are seen on all the island
highways. In wine-pressing season the
WASH baskets often give way to wine
barrels.


GrandmOther's Dresses in STYLE,


Some Of the main streets Of Ter
ceira villages are paved with punaice
blocks and thanked with neat cutters.
Beyond the cutters are smooth pave
ments Of mosaics. Now and then the
black ana white blocks spell . name
familiar to the islanders or form a
beautiful design.


After glance at those who tread
the mosaics it would be hard to con-
vince stranger that Terceira Is about
midway between Paris and New York

for these two fashion centers have had

ority over Italy with the latter's claim

raise the problem of naval superiority

ing their respective, long-fought claims.


italians express belief that Italy will

The Senate subcommittee on District
appropriations evidently has sought to
settle the controversy over the Michigan
avenue grade crossing, but the proce-
dure adopted remains something of a
mystery pending the emergence from
committee of the appropriations bill.
Senator Bingham yesterday introduced,
and the bill was Immediately consid-
cred and favorably reported from the
District committee, a measure author
iZing an appropriation of $780, 900 for
o Michigan avenue grade crossing along
the line of the new and widened Mich
igan avenue. The appropriations bill as
It came from the House appropriated
$135,000 for reconstruction of the Mon
roe street overpass over the B. g. o.
tracks and did not mention Michigan
avenue. Interest now lies in whether
the Senate committee plans to have
both projects undertaken. or whether
the Michigan avenue proposal is to be
substituted for the Monroe street over
pass plan.


There has been some controversy be-
tween the Park and Planning Commits
sion and the municipal authorities over
the Embarrassing elimination. The
municipal authorities have favored
strengthening and widening the Monroe
street overpass, routing Michigan ave-
nue. traffic over Monroe street and clos
ing Michigan avenue at the grade cross
ing. The Park and Planning Commits
sion has favored going forward with the
widening of Michigan avenue immedi-
ately. and has regarded the Monroe
street widening proposal as rather poor
economy. There has been no disagree
ment between the two agencies as 10
the eventual necessity of the Michigan
avenue proposal, but the municipal
heads evidently took the view that
straitened finances required postponing
the Michigan avenue plan, while the
Monroe street scheme, also necessary
should be started now.


The Park and Planning Commission
fears that If the Michigan avenue
widening and Embarrassing proposal Is
side-tracked, it might be postponed Tor
many years. If the Senate appropria-
tions committee proposes to switch from
the Monroe street plan to the Michigan
avenue plan, the completion OF the
latter viii require some time, possibly
two years. If both undertakings are
contemplated. the Senate appropriations
committee must find way to finance
them.


Elimination of the Michigan avenue
grade crossing has been delayed too long
already. Legislation authorizing the
work was enacted in 1927, but the funds
were never appropriated. The new
legislation proposed by Senator Bingham
IL necessary because the act Of 1927
specified the overpass at the site of the
present crossing, while the new plan is
for the crossing along the new route of
Michigan avenue, some distance away.

of his shirt.


Neither Irving nor Bennett would talk

Two others, the driver of the car in

away and the man who trained the
gun on the two store employees, are still
being sought.


Mr.. and Mrs. Arthur Putnam of 1903
Eighth street southeast, who had par
TALLY identified" Irving Friday night,

staged the hold-up.

five and ten cent store when Earl D.
Flory and Harvey w. Smith, the two
store employees were robbed of the days
receipts, which they were taking to the
bank for deposit.

followed the car used by the hold-up
men as far as Stanton Park before
the latter finally dissuaded her hus-
band from continuing the pursuit.


Flory and Smith were given another
look at the two suspects, but again
failed to identify either. The en-
ployes said they could only identity
the man who pulled the gun on them
as they walked from the store. because
they said they were so badly frightened.

bids at Minneapolis so that no wheat

traces of civilization-camp sites,
shell heaps, burial places, and os-

Special Dispatch to The Star.


NEW YORK, December 12-With q
lifting of the pressure that depressed
Thursdays market, stocks today as q
whole made moderate recovery, but on
reduced volume. There were weak spots
and weak groups. but the industrial
leaders were well supported and ranged
higher. Nervousness over banking de-
velopmentS seemed to have disappeared.
Opening prices were higher, and the
! list maintained a steady tone through
out the forenoon. United States Steel
furnished leadership, selling up some 2
points and holding the gain well.
Whether this was special support or
whether 1t was outside buying, the eff
feet was the same in improving sentf-
ment. American Can, General Electric,
WESTINGHOUSE and General Motors were
ali firm.


COppers and Oils Weak.


The two weak spots were the coppers
and the oils. The copper statistics made
public over night were interpreted un-
favorably ard Anaconda sold OF to q
new low, with Kennecott at approx
mately the old low. There was nothing
new in the oil situation but these stocks
were depressed, with new lows for
Standard OIL of California, Barnsdall
and General Asphalt. Income state
ments at the end of the year are sure
to make unpleasant reading for share
holders, but the outlook was no worse
than 1t has been for long time.


The rally in the rails was hesitant.
Advances brought In fresh offerings and
the result was an irregular movement.
Still, the group as q whole did better.
Chicago e. Northwestern was up q
couple of points and lesser gains were
made by st. Louis-San Francisco, Lack
awanna and Baltimore & Ohio. New
York Central and Atchison were reac-
tionary during the forenoon.


At intervals short covering played O
part in advancing prices. United Fruit,
Union Carbide, Air Reduction, Johns
Manville and National Biscuit were
among the stocks to benefit by this
sort Of buying. Utilities were strong
in the first hour and then sold OF
again. Gains were made in American
81 Foreign Power, in American Water

All this was accomplished, however,
on small turnover. Neither side was
anxious to take the initiative. Profess

TO see how far the rally would 60 and

making new commitments


Although there was considerable short
covering, the outstanding short interest
remained large. It will take tangible
evidence of trade betterment to turn
the market about, and that Is yet to
come. The best that could be said
about today'S session was that condi-
tionS In business were being appraised
without the demoralizing influences of
Thursday when the Bank Of United
States closed its doors


Money renewed ct 2 per cent and was
nrm ct that rate. In the outside mar
ket loans were quoted at az per cent
Thirty million dollars in loans were
called during the morning.


Opening Is Higher.


Evidence of restored confidence was
seen in the brisk rally in early trading.
The nervousness over the banking
troubles had disappeared and buying
orders for both accounts predominated.


The leader on the recovery was United
States Steel, which crossed 141, up over
q point, with similar gains In American
Can and In American Telephone &
Telegraph All of these stocks had been
heavily sold earlier In the week, all had
q large short interest outstanding and
Steel had been loaning at q premium.
Short covering likewise advanced quo
tations for stocks such as United Fruit,
Union Carbide & Carbon, Johns Man
Vile and National Biscuit.


The rails made more modest re-
sponse to the better feeling. But most
Of the changes were upward. Only In
the oils was there any real weakness.
General Asphalt and Barnsdall made
new lows. Sinclair duplicated its pre-
vious low and others in the group were
heavy.


The turnover In the first half hour
was 247, 300 shares. Money renewed at

PORT DARWIN, North Australia,
May 24.-Miss Amy johnson, 23-year-
old British aviatrix, reached this city
this afternoon from Atamboea, Timor,
after a fight of 400 miles across the
Timor Sea.


In SO doing she completed in 19 days
a flight alone from Croydon. England.
She left there May s, hoping to beat
Bert Hinkler's record of a 15-day fight
from island to continent, but bad
weather and accidents delayed her in
the latter stages of her trip, and she
fell behind her schedule after flying
two days ahead of it for much of the
journey.


A large crowd which had gathered
cheered her until they we're hoarse.


Government officials were among
those greeting the pretty young girl.
When the official ceremony was over,
they hurried her off in motor car to
Government House, where she win be
the guest of the North Australian gov
ernment during her stay here.


She was very tired, very brown from
the sun and quite deaf after the long
hours behind the roaring motor of her
plane. She said the flight from Timor
was uneventful except for a heavy wind
which carried her slightly off her course.


Her time was about the same that
most other flyers use for the trip. She
lost two days en- route at Rangoon due
to plane injury and another day at
Tjomal near Surabay, when she had to
Land ina sugar clearing and bamboo
spikes tore her wing fabric.

That Peter the Great Of Russia was
able to take as wife an ignorant peasant
girl was due to a centuries-old custom
which had prevailed in Russia.


That country, in its earlier crudeness,
unable to obtain for its sovereigns alli-
ance with the royal houses of neighbour
ing countries, borrowed a veritable Gin
derella- making institution from the By
zantines. 1t had its political advantages.
When wife was desired for the Gar,
or his heir apparent, $500 beautiful
maidens were gathered from all sections
and taken to Moscow that the husband
to-be might make his own selection.


Peters own mother, Nathalia Kiril-
Iowa, had been such a Cinderella.


The Gar Alexis, his father, had lost
his first wife, the Princess Marie Him
itchna Misoslavsky, after she had borne
him Is children. Eleven of these died,
and in 1870 the only heirs of Alexis
were his two sons, Theodore, who was so
sickly that it was not believed he would
live, and Ivan, who was almost an idiot.
Russian peasants knew that the Gar
would be certain to marry again and
began to prepare their daughters for the
traditional ceremony.


Their efforts counted for naught.
One evening while the Gear was at the
house of Artemon Sergheievitch Mat
veief, his chief minister, he lost his
heart. When Mime. Matveief entered
the room in which the Gar sat, bring
ing the vodka, the caviar, the smoked
fish and the other appetizers Russians
employ before embarking upon supper,
she was assisted by a black-eyed young
beauty. This was ward of Matveief.

For street and general daytime wear

selves to careful tailoring. TweedS are

loosen, and lacy tweedS are considered

cialized wear.


The rough tweeds make topcoats

steamer wear and so light in weight

loosely woven, lacy tweeds lend them
selves charmingly to the bright colors
that are peculiarly appropriate for re-

In a quaint brick house on Fifth
street, amid the hallowed memories
OF colorful past, sits little gray
haired widow, whose veneration of the
dead has led her to preserve to this
day the old mahogany bar, brass rail,
beer mugs and other accessories of her
late husbands prohibition calling.


"Morman's" once was a name with
which to conjure Mention of the
name will quicken long dormant mem
cries of many veteran of the in
GereStlng days when horse cars passed
down the Avenue, gas lamps f1ickered
above the heads of the old corner
gang" and conviviality reigned be-
hind inviting swinging doors


Few old-timerS who once tilted mugs
and exchanged pleasantries over the
hoSpitable bar which Eddie Norman
kept on the alley corner near Fifth
and I streets know that the self-same
sign, emblaZoned with the single word,
"Mormanns." remains today-ablaze
with the new gilt of a recent over
hauling.


Painters whom Mrs. Norman en-
gagged to redecorate the old house this
Summer sought to dismantle the VEN
cradle sign, but the kindly old lady
stood her ground and today the sign
continues to spread its message of an
cient good cheer.


Remnants Carefully Stored.


There was something Mrs Mormann
did not ten the painters, and that she
has not divulged to many of her friends.
In room in the basement of her home,
behind lock and key, are stored all
remnants of the glory that once was
Mormann's


If prohibition were to be lifted TODAY
the old bar room could be promptly re-
stored to its appearance of more than a
decade ago. Not that Mrs. Norman
believes and desires that the old DAYS
might return-neither she nor her nus
band were opponents of prohibition. In
fact, 1t was not the prohibition law that
caused Eddie Norman to lock his doors
and draw his shades and store his bar
room equipment. Mormann's closed two
years before the prohibition era because
OF regulation against proximity of
saloons to churches. There were two
churches of different denominations
within few blocks of Mormanns place.


Room Eventually Shorn.


Eddie Norman left things pretty
much as they were in the old bar room
for several years, but eventually he had
the room shorn of all its familiar
furnishings with the exception of two
cut-glass pendant chandeliers, which
once shed their mellow gas light upon
the joyous scenes below. The long bar
was divided into sections, the rail was
removed, the sturdy tables and chairs
were packed up, mugs and glasses were
boxed and even the inevitable froth
SUCK was preserved. Everything was
piled high in the improvised storage
room, the door was padlocked and
Eddie Norman turned to less interest
ing pursuits in friends restaurant.


Mr.. Norman passed away in the old
mouse OF his former associations about
three years ago, at the ripe age of rs
years. Fffty-three years he had been
In the bar room business-all but is
OF those years being spent on the Fifth
street alley corner.


He bequeathed the old house, with all
its glamorouS possessions, to his beloved
and faithful companion of those happy
years. companion who, behind the
scenes, had helped him with the oysters
and the free lunches and had been his
faithful helpmeet through times Of
early stress and Of later prosperity.


NOW Mrs. Norman, who is 70 years
old, lives in the house with her only
child, a daughter, who has a grown,
married daughter of her own. Recently
the daughter went to California to visit
her daughter and the latter's husband,
and Mrs. Norman was left alone, save
for the presence of several roomers on
the floors above.


Yes" the soft-voiced old lady sighed
when visited by q reporter, "it's pretty
lonesome here without my daughter
and without Eddie. But the knowledge
tnat Eddie's most priced belongings are
nearby is a thought that consoles and
comforts me as nothing else can

Less than a month from today, 13-

jealous sutton who later ended his life.
will walk from Casualty Hospital suffi-
GENTLY recovered to return to her FAM
lily at 923 B street, attending ply
sicians predicted yesterday.


And when she bids farewell to nurses
and doctors who stood by her night and
day, she will carry two leaden slugs
with her, one lodged just beneath the
skin under the right eye and the other
in the muscles of her back.


The bullets fired into her body by
Ross Golden, 29-year-old World War
veteran, during jealous rage, will re-
main in place for six months. A Sec
ond operation then will be performed
to remove them.


Hope Was Nearly Gone.


Practically all hope for Che life of
the blonde schoolgirl had been given
up when she was first placed on the
operating table of the hospital. Doctors
told her family that their childs life
hung by thread.


DR.. c. J. Murphy. after performing
the operation, spent the first night
watching over the girl.


In the morning she awoke and asked
for her family. And with their ar
rival her strength seemed to double.


Doctors considered a blood trans
fusion and several hours later her
father Charles J. Raft, was selected
from scores Of volunteers to undergo
blood test Two pints of blood were
t"ken from the father and injected into
her veins.


The next day the girl showed signs
OF improvement. Doctors expressed
surprise that patient so seriously in
jured should rally so rapidly.


Yesterday the girl was in the best
Of spirits. She smiled wanly when
doctors told her to look pretty for
the news photographers


Grimace Conquered by Pluck.


A grimace which clouded her face
when they propped her up in bed for
the cameramen was conquered by the
same pluck that helped her in her battle
with death and the wan smile returned.


Members of the girls family have
kept an almost constant vigil at the
hospital.


Although the girl is suffering from
peritonitis, physicians say they have
the disease under control and within
the next few weeks expect complete
cure. They said her breathing is regu-
lar, her pulse normal, and her tempera-
ture fair.

The western part Of Massachusetts,
from the Connecticut line to the Yer
mont line has long been famous as q
region of great scenic charm. This
section Is known as the Berkshire
Hills, which are part of the great APP
palachian Mountain Range, which
stretches across the Eastern part of
the country. These hills are very diff
ferent in character, however, from the
rest of the range. Their charm is
unique; and in atmosphere they re-
semble the lake country of England far
more than they do the Appalachian
or the White Mountains, which they
link together.


A trip up to the Berkshire Hills is
one of real enjoyment and the urge to
return several times year always re-
mains. The region is ideal, Spring,
Summer and Fall.


In this article the Automobile Club
of America has outlined various routes
not only from New York City into the

also plan to include this region in their
itineraries when making their usual
vacation trip.


Attractive New York Route.


From New York one round trip that

along the Hudson River through
Yonkers, Tarrytown, Peekskill, Pough-
keepsie, Red Hook, Hudson and East
Greenbush into Troy. From here the
Taconic Trail over Petersburg Noun

This road has been opened only a few

Then from Williamstown the Mohawk

home Of Smith College, and then over
the Berkshire Trail through Leeds,
Windsor and Dalton into Pittsfield.
From PittS1eld turn south through the
famous villages Of the Berkshire region
-Lenox, Stockbridge and Great Bar
rington into Canaan, Conn. From here
run over to Norfolk, then through
South Norfolk into Torrington, and
down the Naugatuck Valley into Water

Another scenic route and one that is
very popular leading into the Berk-

South Egremont and over to Great
Darlington. This route could be used

Pittsfleld and past Pontoosuc Lake to
Wlliamstown. Here one could, &C

North Adams, Charlemont and Shell

ern part of that province, near Ping

CURITYBA, Parana, Brazil, october
22.-InSurgent light horse, trooping
down from the hills of Minas Geraes,
for the second time have cut the rail-
road and other communication be-
tween Sac Paulo and Rio de Janeiro.


A small force yesterday attacked and
occupied Cruzeiro, junction city, about
125 miles from Rio de Janeiro. Advices
received here said the city was de-
Tended by a strong federal force un-
der Capt. Newton Cavalcanti. but did
not indicate extent Of fighting.


Raiders Beaten Back.


At inception of the revolution small
rataing force rode down from Minas
Geraes and occupied Lorena, Just south
Of Curzeiro. It interrupted rail- service
between the republics two chief cities,
but later was beaten back.


The narrow stretch of federal terri
tory between the two cities, comprising
little more than the coastal belt, is al
ways open to such attacks, any one OF
which might have most important MILF
tary consequences.


Arrival here of Getulio Vargas, CONF
manding the rebel armies, en- route to
the front, has revivified this little city.
Multitudes besteged his hotel during
the night, demanding he address them.
Vargas, who was defeated by Julio
Prestes for the presidency of the Brazil
ian Union in the last national election,
generally spurned the popular homage
and spent his time preparing plans for
his campaign along the Sac Paulo-
Parana front.


Attended Celebration.


He did, however, attend celebration
of Curityba women, where he shared
honors with Anita Garibaldi, grand
daughter of the Italian lberator.


Streets here are alive with activity,
both of soldiery moving to the front
and of citizens engaged in war prepare
tions. Among other movements is one
of raising funds and sending supplies
to families Of poor soldiers engaged in
the fighting.

ALSDORF, Rhenish Prussia, October
22.-This mining town of 10000 inhabi-
tants was plunged into new grief to-
day, when the realization struck home
that there was no hope for 81 miners
still under ground in the Anna II coal
mine. With certain death total OF
23l and the bodies of ITO victims of
yesterdays mysterious explosion already
recovered, there seemed every likelihood
this afternoon that further increases
in the death list must be made.


Ninety-nine persons remained in hos
pitfalls, many of them being in critical
condition.


CHASTITY Sight Greets Rescuers.


When rescue crews, wearing gas
masks, penetrated to a pit 1900 feet
below the surface, a CHASTITY sight met
their eyes. All about them the VIC
tins lay, apparently asphyxiated. From
this pit not one person had emerged
alive. 1t was only then that the would
be rescuerS realized hope must be given
up for any others in that area.


There were heartbreaking scenes as
the dead were taken from the shaft and
their families identified them. Many
persons came from surrounding towns
some even motoring over the nearby
Belgian and Dutch bordersA These
thronged the town today, but a strong
force of mounted and foot police kept
the crowds at distance from the mine.


Seek Cause of Blast.


A government commission continued
its efforts to learn the cause of the
explosion. The blast at f1rst was at
tributed to ignition of dynamite. Coal
damp also was suspected, but it was the
belief that this latter deadly factor
had not entered into the tragedy that
encouraged those above ground for
many hours in the belief that large
numbers of the miners would be res
cued alive from the deep but well VEN
tilated galleries.

Broadcasting stations owned by re-
ligious institutions are gradually yield
ing their places in the radio spectrum
to commercial interests. In recent
months no less than seven church sta
tons were sold and the transfer of their
licenses ratified by the Federal Radio
Commission.


Efforts of other church groups to find
a Judgement in radio are almost invari-
ably resisted by the commission, which
has shown a decided preference for
stations furnishing an all-around pro-
gram service rather than for those
with highly specialized messages. How
ever, even before the commission came
into being there were about so stations
owned by churches, theological schools
or evangeliStS.


The ranks of the so are slowly being
depleted, though some of the religious
stations, notably those owned and oper-
ated by evangelists, show no disposition
whatever to abandon radio. For the
most part churches are depending for
radio outlets upon affiliations with
tier local broadcasting stations, while
their national organizations are being
heard over the radio networks.


The church stations which recently
abandoned or offered to abandon their
licenses to commercial enterprises were
the following: WABI, First Universalist
Church, Bangor, Me-; WGBC, First
Baptist Church, Memphis. Tenn;
WNBJ, Lonsdale Baptist Church, Knox
vile, Tenn; WEMC, Emanuel Mis-
sionary College, Berrien Springs, Mich;
KGFG, Faith Tabernacle Association,
Oklahoma City: WDAH, Trinity Metho-
dist Church, Ell PaSo, Tex, and KQW,
First Baptist Church, San Jose, Calf.


Most church stations are local, low
powered affairs. Among the Sects rep
resented in the list of those remaining
are the Baptists. Methodists, Presby-
terians, Catholics Congregationalists,
Lutherans and Seventh-day Adventists.


Only few have 1000 watts or more
power, and these almost invariably are
on the air only part time as. for ex-
ample, WLWL, Kearny, N. j., owned
by the Paulist Fathers, which broad
casts only from 6 to 8 pm. daily;
WBBR, New York, and WORD, Ba-
tavia, Ill, owned by the Peoples Pulpit
Association, each sharing time three
ways with nearby stations; WMBI. Chi
cago Moody Bible Institute, which shares
time with WCBD, Zion, Ill, owned by
Wilbur Glenn, Voliva, and KTBI, Los
Angeles, owned by Aimee Semple Nc
Pherson, which shares with KGEF. Los
Angeles, owned by the Trinity Metho-
dist Church


Only a few of the church stations
themselves sell time" to commercial
sponsors of programs. Except for the
evangelists, who often solicit funds for
their stations over the air, the church
stations have found the economic bur-
den of operating broadcasting stations
too great for them. This accounts for
the willingness of many of them to sell
out On the other hand, others, like
the Peoples Pulpit Association and
Wilbur Glenn Voliva, have persistently
sought better wave lengths and more
time on the air from the Federal au-
thorities.
