SPEYER. Germany, July ls-Presi-
dent Won Hindenburgs first day in the
liberated Rhineland was the occasion
for the warmest reception accorded any
German in this ancient city since the
republic was founded.


From early morning, when the presi-
Dental car pulled into the railway sta
ton and until his departure for Lud-
wigshafen, Worms and Mayence in the
early afternoon, crowds such as Speyer
has seldom witnessed thronged the
streets and burst into frantic applause
every time the revered head Of the ma
ton showed himself.


At the city hall, where the President
responded to the official greetings of
the Bavarian and Badenese premiers,
the crowds standing outside shouted
so insistently that the soldier states
man had to show himself on the bal
cony and wave to the multitude, which
spontaneously broke into the strains Of
Deutschland Uber Allies"


The octogenarian President surprised
everybody by the erectnesS of his bear
ing and the firmneSs Of his voice. He
looked At and we'll.


In the Presidents encourage were For
eign Minister Julius Curtius, the Presi-
dents SON and aide, Col. Oscar Van
Hindenburg, and his political secretary,
DR.. Otto Meissner. The President again
scorned taking physician along.


From Speyer President Won linden
burg started by automobile through the
Palatinate for Ludwigshafen, from
where Rhine steamer was to carry
him via Worms to Mayence. His entire
trip Is to consume five days.


MAYENCE, Germany, July 10 CP).-
President Won Hindenburg, making an
almost royalty triumphal progress
through the newly liberated Rhineland,
landed here this evening from a river
steamer that had brought him from
Ludwigshaven.


All river boats were gaily beflagged.
The city, only last month evacuated by
the French army of occupation, was in
holiday mood.


The President. wearing o black
Prince Albert coat and a top hat, was
received by city authorities and after
supper with a few intimate friends
| retired to the palace, where Napoleon
once stayed and where Gen. Guillaumat,
commander of the French occupying
groups, had his headquarters.
Won HindenburgS journey today bore
witness to his extraordinary popularity
The whole countryside turned out TO
pay him homage. For miles the roads
were lined by peasants Justify cheering
the presidential automobile.
Except for a few odd box cars stand
| ing idle in freight yards, and one or two
sign posts with French directions, all
public signs of the French occupation
have vanished from this area.

munists in the large crowd, the officers

WELLINGTON, New Zealand, August
18.-The MatSon liner Ventura wire
Iessed today that all passengers, officers
and crew of the British steamer Tahiti,

About SO other bags were badly

saved.

sost.


The Ventura had rushed from many
miles away to answer the Tahiti's dis

tura. Launching of the boats was not
:. without danger, for although the
weather was fair, heavy swell was
running. OfhcerS believed the ship

ming, local time, it remained along

forenoon.

Digging a hole through the jail
wall and scaling the outer walls,

escape from the Rockville jail
early today.


Posses have been securing the
country, but SO far have not
picked up their trail.

Ter, serving a term of four years,
and William Jones. serving ID
months. Both men were con-
victed of houSebreaking and en-.
tered the Jail two months ago.


Dig Hole in Wall


Last night the men ripped the
iron rods from their cots and used
them as crowbarS.


They managed to dig hole In
the side of the jail large enough
to wriggle through. Jumping to
the ground, they ran across the
Jail yard, scaled the wall and
made their escape.


A truSty heard them going over
the wall and called the night
guard who discovered the break
and gave the alarm.


On Second Floor


According to j. E. Mosley,
jailer, the two men made their
getaway about $3.50 o'clock this
morning. Their cell was on the
second floor.


Eight Escape in Three Years


The number of men escaping
the last three years has now
reached the total of eight. Only
one has been returned. The jail
was built in 1852 and it will soon
be replaced by a stronger jail
in the new courthouse now being

LONDON, England, January 27.-The
fundamental Franco-Italian divergence
broke out with full force in Downing
street today at the meeting of the i've
powers delegates to draft an agenda for
the Naval Conference and occupied the
delegates during three entire hours. The
Americans, seconded by the British,
acted throughout as tactful concili-
atoGs and were instrumental in causing
the adoption of a compromise solution
which finally permitted the delegates to
go to luncheon at 1870 o'clock.


The issue was seemingly insignificant.
The French proposed that the agenda
should begin with the discussion or
global tonnage and tonnage transfers
The Italians, who demanded parity with
France, suspected the French of a ma
neuver-namely, to make each nation
present its figures, examine the figures
in the light of actual possibility, demon
strate that the French possibilities and
needs are greater than the Italian, fix
the ratios on this basis and keep Italy
lower than France. They therefore
proposed that the agenda begin with a
discussion of ratios and the fixing of
maximum tonnage levels.


Expected Italian Maneuver.


The French, who cannot formally re-
fuse parity to Italy, but who intend to
set the figures so high that Italy can
not afford TO follow, suspected the ItaI-
ians of the following maneuver: To FIX
the ratios on the basis of the. Washing
ton treaty, which in capital ships gives
Italy parity with France, and fix the
tonnage maximum Immediately at such
low level that Italy can afford to
build up to France. They therefore Wig
orously resisted the Italian thesis.


The solution finally voted, after
three hours Of hard wrangline. in
which there was no time to raise
any other topic, was that all the points
Italians should be discussed. but in
alphabetical order, according to the
power proposing the subject. As France
begins with F and Italy with I. this
gives France precedence. This com
promise, however, obviously settles
nothing. The issue remains entire.


japanese Delegates FESTIVE.


The British are therefore meeting the
French and Italians at 4:3O O'clock
this afternoon, after which the British
and French alone will pow-pow.


AS result of these Developments the
meeting scheduled for this afternoon
between the British and the Japanese
has been postponed until tomorrow.


The Japanese delegates appear more
ana more FESTIVE, for reasons which
NOBODY seems able exactly to explain.
SINCE no fundamental issue has yet
been discussed, and the Japanese de-
mands thus far have been neither
granted nor refused.

By the Associated Press.


SPRINGFIELD, Ohio, October TO-
Vice President Charles Curtis, speaking
here last night at dinner ignoring
the memory of George Rogers Clark,
paid high tribute to the courage and
bravery of Clark, Daniel Boone and
other pioneers whose deeds made pos
sible the opening Of the great North
west Territory for settlement century
ago.


The Vice President said the spirit
that prompted Clark and his fellow
pioneers to push ahead into the wilder
ness amid great dangers from maraud-
ing Indians and animals, is carried on
today by the feats Of Lindbergh, Byrd
and Edison, to whom the present gen.
Grafton pays homage.


Tracing the history of Clark's expedi-
ton to the battle of Piqua, fought near
here, where Clark and his command
routed the Indians and destroyed their
villages, Vice President Curtis said that
they were propelled by desire to open
new territory and establish new cities.


Curtis pointed out that the Indians
finally laid down their arms and
adopted the habits and dress of the
white man under a program Of peace
full persuasion"


This is not the time nor the place
to discuss the Indian question" he
said, "but I must say our officials in
washington and their representatives
in the field have made many mistakes
in their dealings with the Indian
tribes.


Had treaties, obligations and prom
ises been more sacredly kept and a
greater effort made to give the Indians
better school and vocational training
the Indian question would have been
solved years and years ago."

DHARASANA, InS.s. May 21.-Tor

Today's raid was featured by q stra-

surged about these until the police

Cushioned only by excellent backloGs
in line pipe in the Pittsburgh and
Youngstown districts and by moderate
backlogs in ship plates in Eastern Penn
sylvania, finished steel demand and pro-
duction have retreated further this
week, says the Iron Trade Review,
Cleveland.


Current requirements of majority Of
steel consumers are lighter, and interest
in the third quarter is negligible, espe-
cially in those districts placing major
reliance upon automotive, railroad and
farm implement business.


Smokestacks of some Mahoning VAL
ley sheet mills already are rusty, and
July and August promise to be the low
est months of the year in automotive
demand, largely because of shutdowns
contemplated by Ford and other impor-
tant interests.


Freight car builders at Chicago have
practically worked of their orders, and
have inquiry for only 5000 cars before
them. Implement manufacturers ap!
proach inventory time with large stocks.
In the past few days there has been q
noticeable depression of sentiment In
quarters where week or two ago some
hopes for improvement were voiced.


Steel prices continue irregular and
vulnerable to concessions. but the lack
of buying and consequent pressure gives
the market Semblance of stability
Producers, however, feel that prices in
the main will 60 little lower, and while
willing to contract a short distance into
the third quarter, are avoiding long
term commitments that would preclude
taking advantage of any strength that
developed late next quarter. Some quo
tations are not far above costs.


Though the price situation still con-
tains soft spots, the lack of buying
cloakS them. AS result the Iron Trade
Review composite is unchanged this
week at 1882. It's average for May
was $SS.73 and for last June 1864.

A young pilot and his girl passenger
escaped with trivial hurts yesterday
afternoon when their biplane over
turned on a plowed field near Berwyn
Heights during an emergency landing,
which catapulted the youth from the
machine and left the girl dangling
head down from the passenger cockpit.


1t was Miss Rose Parks first ride
Miss Park, who is 20 years old and
lives at 1716 Irving street, drove to
College Park Airport with her mother,
who watched while she was helped into
the plane. Plotted by Eli Amanuel, 23-
year-old member of the District Air Le-
gion and a musician employed in the
Mayflower Hotel Orchestra, the machine
took off for short hop.


Motor Stalls in Air.


The motor stalled about mile from
the airport and spectators there, in
Guiding Mrs. Park, saw the plane de-
scend suddenly from a height of sew
eral hundred feet. Amanuel managed
to clear the trees beneath and headed
for the small field.


AS the machine came in with the
wind behind it, wing hit some small
trees. The plane bounced on the muddy
ground and Hoped over. Amanuel,
thrown from the cockpit, released the
safety belt which vas holding Miss Park
in and helped her from the machine.


Fearing that Mrs. Park had seen the
plane descend and would believe her
daughter killed, Amanuel helped the
girl on a short cut for the field through
a swamp. The plane landed not far
from the engine house of the BerWyn
Heights Fire Company and that ap-
paratus was quickly on the scene.


Firemen Give Aid.


Firemen assisted the couple from the
swamp while some one ran to telephone
that they were only slightly injured.
The fire rescue squad from Bladensburg
also was summoned to the scene. Fire
men gave Miss Park first aid for black
right eye and Amanuel for cut lip.
Both then returned to the field.


The plane is the property of the Dis
trict Air Legion. Badly damaged, it was
dismantled and returned to the flying
field


Amanuel had rented the plane from
the legion to accede to a request to take
Miss Park aloft. He has been flying
for about two years and was licensed.
Amanuel lives at 4806 Kansas avenue.

ISTANBUL, Turkey, June 10.-A
treaty of friendship between Turkey and
Greece was signed here today.


The agreement was signed by the
Turkish foreign minister, DR.. Tevfik
Rushdi Bey and the Greek minister at
Angora, M. Polychroniadis.


The long awaited agreement was con-
sidered prelude to Turko Greek amity
pactS, entailing trip of Premier Veni-
zelos in october to Angora.


The Turkish press said that consum-
nation of the friendship agreement
made the Turkish horizon more peaceful
than it had been for six centuries.
Twenty thousand Greeks in Istanbul,
who under the accord are recognized
as established residents, especially well
coined the treaty. During the last seven
years inability of the two nations to
agree upon their status has made them
officially lost souls" unable to pro-

PITTSBURGH, October A woman
and two men were shot and killed and
another man was wounded probably
fatally today when gangsters' guns were
fired five times in little grocery store
in Braddock, suburb.


Two men fired with deadly precision
to kill Joseph Lobianco, proprietor of
the store, his 27-year-old wife, and
Louis Tomano, 70, a customer. Lobian-
cos brother, Michael, %. was wounded
so seriously he was not expected to
live.


Residents of the neighborhood said
three men drove up to the store shortly
after 8 am. and while one remained at
the wheel Of their automobile the other
two entered the store. Shots were
heard and the gunner ran out, leaped
into the automobile and sped away.


Pedestrians ran into the store and
found Lobianco dead with a bullet
wound in the abdomen. His wife was
wounded similarly. She and Tomano
died short time later.


Lobianco opened his small grocery
store three weeks ago.


County detectives believed that the
shooting resulted from emmity caused
by liquor dealings involving Lobianco
or jealousy over Mrs. Lobianco.


The officers began search for a
large red sedan. An automobile Of that
description was used by the slayers.
The machine was reported found later
in North Braddock.

CHICAGO, October 16.--A suburban

unwilling medium through which gang

investigator to have acted in good faith,
was not detained.


"It is through the gullibility of small
town police chiefs that gangsters get
most of these weapons" Roche said.

The electric street railroads of the
country are prepared to call for a show
down on the street traffic congestion
situation. This was learned yesterday
from executives of the companies, who
are now making their way toward San
Francisco, where the American Electric
Railway Association will meet Monday


The situation affects every city and
hamlet in the country, as we'll as the
street car lines, which operate some 30
per cent OF the urban public utility
transportation.


Downtown Parking.


Downtown parking is the foremost
problem. The street car men say the
time has come when streets can no
longer be used for motor car storage.
They are advocating free movement for
all vehicles. This question has threat
ened to stir up a controversy in Presi-
dent Hoover's street and highway safety
conference, but it has never been dis
cuSsed so openly and frankly as it will
be at San Francisco.


Arrayed on one side are the city
planners and public transportation men,
They insist all streets should be used
only for moving traffic. On the other
side are the motor car men and many
Of the merchants.


The first group asserts that the cost
OF new streets and widening of old
thoroughfares should not be placed on
taxpayers until existing streets are used
to capacity for moving traffic. They
insist that the whole problem should
be handled on city planning basis and
that the erection of Skyscrapers, which
figure largely in the production of con-
gestion, should be taken into considera-
ton. They cite highway accident rec
ords as an argument against haphazard
traffic control. While auto accidents
have increased, street car facilities have
dropped.


Charges Disputed.


The electric railway and bus men
argue that since they carry three pas
sengers to every one carried by private
autos, and carry them more safely they
streets.


The second group does not see eye
to eye with the street car and bus men.
Automobile men say they are doing
everything possible to prevent accidents
They say that if parking space is not
available at curbS, the cities should
build downtown garages and provide
free parking service. Street widening
and the building of new streets are
inevitable, they declare.


Many merchants believe abolition OF
street parking would hurt their trade
They would rather see one car parked
before a store than dozen rolling past.
despite assertions that Chicago mer-
chants have found abolition of park
ing help to trade. A Chicago survey
showed 1.06 per cent of trade came from
parkers.

The colored men slain were John

The colored men, Tom Robertson and

and 800 armed men after they had
beaten up Clarence Boyd, nephew of

A coroner's jury late today returned

came to their death at the hands of
party or parties unknown" Oficials
mad made no indication that an investi-
CATION would be conducted


Jim Ayres. white, was suffering cheek

Boyd, nephew of Grover, was injured

held by colored man.


First reports of the trouble were ex-
aggerated, the death list being given as
high as eight.


Dead and 2 Wounded.


Sheriff w. D. Scales who took charge
OF the search last night and attempted
to control the unruly mob of 200 to 300
men, today checked the casualties and
found four dead and two wounded.


Reports that two colored men had
been burned to death also were proved
un1ounded by search of the ruins of
John Robertson'S home.


The trouble started late yesterday
when Clarence Boyd met Esau Robert
son and demanded payment for a stor-
age battery he had sold him.


The colored man said he did not have
the money, and Boyd seized the battery.





the store in which they were standing

ance and one of the colored men fired

Most American editorialists pointed

and almost bloodless manner in which

Bolivia, Peru and Argentina astounded
American newspapers. They were not
used to It.


Well, here we have again the colorful
and violent, the fiery revolution they
were looking for. While these lines are
being written stormy civil strife Is
sweeping over the vast territory Of
Brazil, the largest South American
country. Bloody rioting has taken

and rebel forces have exchanged well
aimed shots and the whole country Is
o bonfire Of political rivalry and pas
sionate turmoil.


This time, however, we are in the
presence Of q rather different phenom-

of armed warfare or in the number Of
casualties that the Brazilian revolution
differs from those in Bolivia, Peru and
Argentina. It Is also different in prin-

the other. Although at such an enor-
nous distance it is difficult to appreci-
ate the situation and grasp the real

that made possible the almost peace

principles and democratic ideals do not

Learned Ways of the West.
IF Joan Crawford didn't gain any
thing else during the several weeks
she spent In San Jacinto Mountain
cattle ranges during filming Of her
latest Metro-GoldwynM Mayer all-talk-
ing vehicle, Montana Moon" she at
least learned the why's and wherefores
of the traditional American cowboy
regalia.


Among the things she learned is
that the five-gallon sombrero is worn
to protect the eyes from the sun glare,
hail and rain, its wide brim afford
ing protection to both head and Shout
about the throat to serve as a hand
kerchief and to protect the mouth and
nose from alkali particles in dust storms
not only for warmth and to shield the
vent denim trousers from being torn
and, most important, to serve as an
armor against rattlesnake bites.


Miss Crawford was also informed
that the cowpunchers wear high
heeled leather boots because they pre-
vent chatting, the odd-shaped heels
clinching the feet into the stirrups
for hard service; that revolvers are not
carried for protection against bad
men" but for the purpose Of killing
steers or horses and to be used
to check maddened beasts in STAN
pedes; and finally. that lassoes were
used. not to string up cattle thieves, but
to rope steers that are to be picked out
from herds and to bind them for brand
ing.

I read about the golden wedding of
James and Julia Dingbat-Dove, who've
come through good and evil Shedding
to green old age, and still in love. In
life's bright morning they were mar
ried, a blooming maid, a handsome
boy; and neighbors at the altar tarried
to wish them forty kinds of joy. The
woman is no longer blooming, the eager
pep of youth has died, the busy years
have been entombing the charms and
graces of the bride The man is bald
and bent and beaten, long whiskers
hang, his chin beneath; and any grub
he may have eaten was chewed with
cheap mail order teeth. And they are
cheerful and contented. while yet they
watch the swift years fly; the greatest
blessing yet invented is theirs-a love
that does not die. Together in their
sunny morning they faced whatever
life might bring; together now they
face the warning that life approaches
evening. No doubt they've had their
bitter quarrels, the scraps that mar
ried people know; perhaps the man
forgot his morals and cussed around
an hour or So Perhaps the woman
could not smother, at times, the grief
that made her groan, and said she'd
go home to her mother, and let him run
the ranch alone. Such quarrels ran
their little courses, and were forgotten,
then, like dreams, and no one talked
about divorces, or alimony, or such
schemes. In these brave days some
thin excuses suffice to break the mar
riage tie, and ganders leave their divers
gooses because the latter winked an
eye. And so it's good to read of people
who still uphold the VOWS they made
long since, beneath the village steeple,
when they were young and unafratd.


WALT MASON.

of the amazing structures that are being
erected in various parts of the world. For the
new trend Of church architecture is toward
modern art just as is all architecture, all art
and all phases of the twentieth century life


Although the ritual of the church service
has changed less than have many other things,
the method of church building seems to be keep
ing pace with the times. Balls and trangles
of glass and steel, towers of steel and terra
Gotta, concrete blocks that resemble ware
houses factories, airplane hangers and ele-

resound to the Ave Maria and the Doxology,
and call themselves houses of worship. Are all
the classics of religious art to be cast into
the rubbish heap; rose windows gargoyles,
string courses, Ionic columns and whatnot?


Goethe said that architecture is frozen music.
Beholding some of the modern church archi-
lecture, conservative people vaguely wonder if
they are gazing at some CONCEALED score OF the
latest jazz hit.


Yet it is worthwhile to consider this thing in
the light of the century which has produced it.
Undeniably, there are compensations and ex-
plantations which justify these structures as be-
ing ecclesiastical, though they bear little
semblance to the traditional Gothic style which
has been essentially the architecture of the
Christian religion since the twelfth century.
PERHAPS the most important and most


natural influence Of this change in archi-
tectural style is that of materials. Concrete and
steel has replaced stone masonry. Ponderous
stone walls required massive stone pillars for
support, whereas slender steel columns support
q tremendous weight. Immediately there is a
vast difference in the result.


Stone walls prohibited large window openings,
lest the support withdrawn by large window
space weaken the walls. Steel construction sup
ports itself, and the very window frames add to
the strength of walls.


Thick stone walls resulted in deep easements
which shut out light. Concrete walls allow for
easements flush with the outer walls, letting
IN light


When the famous cathedrals of the old world
were built. men toiled for generations to COM
plete them: manual labor, huge stones hauled
for miles, delicate and tedious chiseling with
handmade tools Today similar structures could
be completed in months: minimum labor, gigan-
tic shoves, derricks and trucks that groan and
rumble and snort with hasty precision and un-
faltering strength.


Building with steel and concrete, the archi-
lecture assumes steel proportions In other
words church architecture has adopted the
slender silhouette. Sweeping curves and slender
reaching columns letting there be light and air;
instead of mass and weight and bulk and dusk.

be false gesture, the modern school con-
tends Why not take advantage Of the geo.
metric designs offered by steel construction2
Barrel vaulting in ceilings is longer essential
to sound construction; steel girders will support
at any angle, provided skilled engineers know
their mathematics Both exterior and interior
designs are in planes and surfaces and forms,

WARRENTON, July Allie Corbin,

Elwood Payne, 81, colored, is in jail

three by shooting the farmer and the
two girls, then setting fire to the ma
chine in which the three lay wounded.
Payne denies all charges.


Physicians today indicated that the
TWO daughters may recover, but hold
out few hopes for Corbin, who was shot
through the head. The two women
were wounded in the neck and head
and were burned severely. Corbin also
was burned seriously.

through the head during an argument

tortown, according to information re-
ceiVed by Sheriff w. S. Wolf. He then

is accused of driving them some dis
lance from the house, then running the
car into field, shooting both young
women and pouring gasoline over them
and the automobile and setting fire to
1t. Payne then disappeared, according

who was able to reach a nearby house
and sound the alarm.

Estelle. though wounded through the
neck, succeeded in dragging her father
and herself from the car before the
machine was destroyed by flames.


Payne, who was captured soon after
ward at his home, Immediately denied
the charges of the two girls. He indi-

Pilot Benjamin Jones' airplane fell

home Of Mrs Elizabeth Kirschner.


Her son, Walter Schneider, was late
in taking his usual afternoon nap. His
bed was directly in the path of the
falling motor.

likely would have been In her room, the

BALTIMORE, Md, December 15.-
Every motion picture theater in the
city was open yesterday for the sake
of charity, the State Sunday closing law
being suspended by police officials. It
was the first time since the World War
that performances for pay were per-
mitted. During the war a few benefit
shows were given to aid the Red Cross.


Managers Of neighborhood houses re-
ported that the matinee crowds were
from two to five times the average for
week days, and heavy attendance was
reported by the downtown theaters.


The entire proceeds are to go to a
special fund for unemployment relief,
TO be administered by Police Commis-
sioner Charles D. Gather in co-opera-
ton with philanthropic agencies. Esti-
mates were that $4,000 or more had
been cleared. Virtually all employees
gave their services free.


The Sunday opening was opposed by
the city Baptist and Methodist minis
ters' conferences.


At Cumberland the City Council had
refused to sanction Sunday movies for
. charity fund, but one house was open
and contributions collected from spec
tators.

EVERETT, Mass, June 7 (P).-Sing
Wong, 40, was shot to death last night
in his laundry while at work. Three
shots were fired through a partition
separating the front of his shop from
the rear, one hitting him in the head.


A neighbor, Mrs. Pauline Trowbridge.
was awakened from her sleep by the
shooting. She said she saw a man leave
the laundry and disappear into an
alley. Police said they believed another
Chinese entered Wong's shop and shot
him down without warning.


Police Commissioner Eugene Hoffman
of Boston, which adioins Everett. today
issued warnings to Chinese leaders that
Tong warfare must not be allowed to
break out. Early yesterday seven shots
were fired into the headquarters of the
Hip Sing Tong in Boston.

LOS ANGELES, october IS. - Sep

rounding towns Roads were soon bar
ricaded by officers from surrounding
towns.

rounded by posse of 200 home guards,

cember. In the present instance, how

affecting sales was the disposition on
the part of prospective purchasers to
await the automobile shows before max
ing their selections. Decreases in both
the month-to-month and yearly conn
parsons were spread generally through
all classes of makes.


Relatively the largest declines were
noted among country dealers. Business
in parts and accessories was also in
smaller volume than q month and 3
year earlier.

The 1o-year-old controversy over
whether Armour, Swift and other pack
ers should limit their activities exclu-
sively to meat packing passed through
another phase yesterday, when the Dis
trict of Columbia Supreme Court over
ruled petition asking dismissal of an
attempt by these groups to obtain modi-
fication of the 1920 consent decree.


The decree was consented to after
the Government had instituted anti
trust proceedings against packers, but
was not put into effect until the1 Su-
preme Court sustained the decree. Then
the packers agreed to limit their busi-
ness, and later asked modification be-
cause of economic and financial de-
velopmentS.


In the decision yesterday Justice
Bailey OF the District Supreme Court
denied petition of the American
Wholesale Grocers' Association asking
dismissal Of the packers petition for
modification. This suit was instituted
because the packers asked modification
so they could be allowed to resume gro
Gerry and retail business,


=. Justice Bailey's decision held that
the packers petition should not be act
ed upon until after full hearing on
the merits of questions involved, and
added that the final determination by
the court may largely depend upon
whether the Government shall consent
to or oppose the proposed modifica-
ton" The Government, although not
questioning the right of the court to
grant modification, has challenged the
packers to produce proof that their
claims are justified.

Since a few days before the storm

From Beaufort their forwarding ad-

Post cards came back from Beaufort, but

been no word.


Maybe, say their friends, the ocean

risings indicated today that 3
dangerous state Of affairs still

The capital continued normal

troops and civil guards apparent
everywhere. Police permission Is
necessary to leave the city and
martial law remained in force
throughout the nation. Telephone
and telegraph communications
were restored for the first time
Since the revolt.

General strikes in eight prov

ences, remaining in the royal

DENVER, Colo, October 18.-An

yesterday in Berkeley Lake, two days
after she had disappeared from her
home. She was the daughter Of City
Detective Leo OLoughlin.

they were considering the possibility
that the child had been murdered and
the body thrown in the lake.


Police late last night arrested one
man for investigation after they had
been told he was seen a week age
within block of the OLoughlin home
attempting to entice two small girls
into his car. Police said they would
question him today and check his past
activities


A preliminary examination Of the
girls body by Deputy Coroner George
Bostwick and w. s. Dennis, city
pathologiSt, disclosed two deep wounds
on the back of her head and bruises on
her left upper arm.

O'Loughlin, was taken to police head
quarters and questioned at length after
the discovery of the body. Frank
OLoughlin, brother of the detective
who roomed at the OLoughlin's, was
also questioned. Neither could throw
light on the girls disappearance.


Mrs. OLoughlin, like her husband
has been suffering a mysterious ailment
for several days. occasioned, she said
by eating tainted food. OLoughlin

lest night.

right ankle.

at the hospital and attending nurses
said the condition of each was "as good
as could be expected" Mrs. Schall was
at her sons bedside, the Senator being
absent from the city. Miss Kreps'
parents visited her yesterday.


Young Schall is midshipman at the
United States Naval Academy.

Two weeks ago, in his Memory Test"
feature on the back cover Of The Sun
day Stars magazine section, Cartoonist
Dick Mansfield asked:


who was the first Washington ball
player to catch q base ball thrown
from the Washington Monument"


That's simple" chorused the fans,
Everybody knows that Gabby Street
was the guy"


The surprise was general when, last
Sunday, Mansfield's answer gave the
name Of Phil Baker and the date as
January 8, 1885.


Thousands had never heard of Phil
Baker. The hoary old-timers recalled
him as q f1rst-class catcher; some re-
membered him as the man who first
tried to catch ball from the Monu-
ment. A few maintained that Mans
field was correct.


Newspaper files were thumbed dill
gently.


They revealed substantially what you
have Just read.


The question is: Did Baker hold the
horsehide long enough to constitute
legal catch? Rules of the diamond
game require that the ball be held only
"momentarily" to complete a play.
